title: Independent Tasks: Problems and Solutions https://curriculumteamleader.wordpress.com/2024/07/02/independent-tasks-problems-and-solutions/
author: Peter Foster
summary: Peter Foster diagnoses the recurring breakdowns that happen when teachers hand independent work over to students, and offers concrete routines for each. For the problem of a class failing to start work, he lays out a reset-and-check sequence: silence the room, verify understanding of instructions through targeted questioning, and only then choose between reteaching via guided practice or simply restarting the task, all while remaining visible at the front to scan the room. For students who get stuck or disengage mid-task, he recommends establishing genuine silence first, narrating expectations explicitly, and using techniques like 'question, don't tell' rather than re-explaining, since re-explaining lets students nod along without revealing whether they actually understood. He also describes using completion problems and worked examples for students who are missing prerequisite knowledge, and setting specific behavioural targets for disengaged-but-capable students. Finally, for the problem of avoidable mistakes surfacing only after the lesson, Foster describes using a laminated seating plan to track which students have been checked, prioritising a planned route around the room, and giving brief in-the-moment feedback rather than stopping the whole class for individual errors unless the pattern is widespread.
points: Foster's reset-and-check sequence for a class that won't start work moves through silence, checking understanding via cold-call questions, and only then choosing between guided reteaching and a straight restart.
He argues 'question, don't tell' beats re-explaining a stuck student's confusion, because re-explaining invites students to nod along out of politeness without revealing real understanding.

He recommends completion problems, borrowed from Cognitive Load Theory, as a middle ground between a full worked example and unsupported independent practice for students missing prerequisite knowledge.
His seating-plan-with-symbols system (cross-through, tick, question mark) turns circulation into a trackable process rather than an ad hoc walk around the room.
quotes: You've got to the point when we want to hand over responsibility to the students. They've got some knowledge; they've handled the component processes and are ready.
Silence in 3... nothing in hands, eyes on me in 2... [scanning the room/thanks to those getting it right] 1... Year 8 that is not what how I said we would conduct ourselves.
Although not all teachers like it, silence is probably the best default for independent tasks.
Sammy Kempner explains this beautifully why it’s important to question rather than tell. We’re eliciting student understanding rather than assuming it.
If you ask questions, students have to answer. These could be questions about the task but can and should also be about the content.
A completion problem, a term borrowed from Cognitive Load Theory, is where the first steps in a problem are completed.

Often teachers will start talking over a class, the minute they see a mistake in one student’s book. This mistake could be important but students are unlikely to listen if you just start talking as they are working.
